newsitem.title: USA: Conservatives deny seeking to unseat Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives deny seeking to unseat Gingrich.

text.p: A group of Republican critics of House Speaker Newt Gingrich reviewed recent public setbacks to their conservative agenda on Tuesday but denied they intended to bring down their leaders.

Representative Mark Souder, Republican of Indiana, said about 50 representatives were dissatisfied with the Republican leadership's response to President Bill Clinton's veto of the disaster relief bill.

Publicity over the invitation-only meeting -- which hinted at a plot to oust Gingrich or other leaders -- was believed to have kept lawmakers away. Organisers rushed to deny any connection with an anonymous letter, which called for a challenge to Gingrich.
"This kind of stuff is not what you take down a speaker over," Souder said of their frustration over the disaster bill. "This is not about the speaker. We need a clear conservative message."

Souder said they were concerned that the conservative message was not being clearly articulated. A delay in sending the disaster-aid bill to the White House gave Clinton three days while they were out of town to blame them for keeping the aid from reaching flood-stricken states.

An organiser of the meeting, Representative Lindsey Graham of South Carolina and Souder pointed out concerns that Republicans might also lose the public relations battle with the White House over coming tax cut legisltion.

"They're (the administration) demagoguing our tax cuts already," Graham said. Souder noted later, "We worry our big victory, which is tax cuts, is going to be snatched from us," by administration complaints that it favours the rich."
This is only the latest in a series of problems to plague Gingrich, who barely won re-election as speaker in January and was reprimanded and fined by his colleagues for ethics violations.
While there was speculation that he might step down from the speakership before his two-year term is up, he did not show signs of that this week.

Many of those frustrated by the pace and direction of leadership were among the freshmen who were elected in 1994 as part of his Republican revolution and remain intent upon cutting the size and cost of government.

In an effort to quell the incipient rebellion, Republican leaders were to stress to their rank-and-file at a Wednesday meeting that the party has made progress on budget issues -- including an agreement to balance the budget in five years, cut taxes and reform entitlement programmes.
Gingrich's top deputy, Majority Leader Richard Armey, applauded the group's effort, calling it a "healthy thing" to discuss how to move the party's agenda forward.
But the Texas Republican pointedly declined to give the speaker a whole-hearted endorsement in response to several questions at his weekly news conference.

In a written statement Armey later defended his actions, saying he had not been asked during the briefing. "Since no one asked, I assumed it was perfectly clear that the leadership continues to be a cohesive team."

By the end of Tuesday, no author had come forward to claim the anonymous letter which cited Gingrich's "blunders" during the 1995 budget battles which left the party bruised by two unpopular government shutdowns. Graham issued a written denial that he was the author.
The letter asked for a vote of confidence in the Republican leadership; a negative vote by the party conference would not automatically result in a recall but would be politically damaging.
